text: Albert Gleizes grew up in Paris as the son of a fabric designer who ran a large industrial design workshop. With Jean Metzinger he wrote the first major treatise on Cubism, Du Cubisme, in 1912. He was a founding member of the Section d'Or, and his theoretical writings were first appreciated in Germany, especially at the Bauhaus. He spent four crucial years in New York and played an important role in making America aware of modern art. From the mid-1920s much of his energy went into writing.

Carle Vernet showed a passion for drawing horses at five and trained under his father Claude-Joseph Vernet. After winning the Prix de Rome in 1782 he seemed to lose interest, and his father had to recall him from Rome to stop him entering a monastery. His sister was executed by guillotine during the Revolution, and he gave up art. When he resumed under the Directory, his style had changed radically, and he drew Napoleon's battles and campaigns in minute detail. Napoleon awarded him the Legion of Honour for his Morning of Austerlitz. Hunting scenes and horses filled his later work.

Frances Hodgkins grew up in Dunedin, where her father was a lawyer and amateur painter active in the city's art circles. She attended the Dunedin School of Art, then taught art to earn money for study in England. In 1890 she first exhibited landscapes and portraits in Christchurch and Dunedin, and in 1893 she became a student of Girolamo Nerli. She worked chiefly in landscape and for a short period designed textiles. Her work is known for abstracted, simplified forms and a strong emphasis on colour relationships.

John Henry Twachtman received his first art training in Cincinnati, including lessons from Frank Duveneck. He enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich in 1875, and his landscapes from then show the loosely brushed, shadowy technique taught there. He also learned etching and sometimes carried plates with him to record a scene spontaneously. Later he studied at the Académie Julian in Paris, and his paintings shifted toward a soft gray and green tonalist style. In 1898 he joined The Ten, a loosely allied group of American artists dissatisfied with professional art organizations.

Johann Elias Haid learned engraving from his father Johann Jacob Haid, who was also his collaborator, and later took over the family publishing business in Augsburg. From 1774 to 1790 he worked on a series of 57 portrait engravings of famous scholars. He later engraved 132 designs by Johann Caspar Füssli for a book on the medals of Johann Carl Hedlinger, which aroused much interest in southern Germany. Although he specialized in portraits, he also engraved works by Frans van Mieris, Bernardo Strozzi and Lucas Cranach.

Willem Swidde came to Stockholm in 1688, recruited by Erik Dahlbergh to illustrate topographical and historical books. His first commission was 18 of the 123 plates for a history of Charles X Gustav of Sweden written by Samuel Pufendorf. His main and final commission, which kept him busy for the rest of his life, was engraving the illustrations for Suecia Antiqua et Hodierna. He made 76 of the book's plates, one of a team of engravers. He worked from drawings by Dahlbergh and often corrected the motifs together with him. He died in Stockholm in 1697.

Ernst Josephson came from a middle-class family of merchants of Jewish ancestry, and his father left home when he was ten. At sixteen he enrolled at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts, where Johan Christoffer Boklund and August Malmström taught him, and in 1876 he received a Royal Medal for painting. He then visited Italy, Germany and the Netherlands with the artist Severin Nilsson to study the Old Masters. A breakthrough came in Paris, where he studied with Jean-Léon Gérôme and concentrated on portraits of fellow Swedes. He also wrote poetry.

Cornelius Varley grew up as the younger brother of the watercolour painter John Varley and was educated by an uncle who made scientific instruments. As a young man he toured Wales with his brother and began to study art. In 1804 he was a founder of the Water-Colour Society. He exhibited occasionally at the Royal Academy until 1859. He mostly painted landscape watercolours, and he also invented the graphic telescope and the graphic microscope.

Maxime Maufra began painting at eighteen, encouraged by the Nantes artists Charles and Alfred Leduc and Charles Le Roux, but he remained a businessman who painted in his spare time. During that period he discovered the Impressionists. In 1890 he gave up business and left Nantes for Pont-Aven in Brittany, where he met Paul Gauguin and Paul Sérusier. His first solo exhibition in Paris followed in 1894, and he later exhibited with Durand-Ruel, who kept him under contract for the rest of his life. He was the first painter to live in the Bateau-Lavoir in Montmartre.

Charles Keene was educated at Ipswich School and showed artistic leanings early. After a spell articled to a London solicitor and then in an architect's office, he spent his spare time drawing historical and nautical subjects in watercolor. His mother found a buyer for these, which brought him to the notice of the wood-engravers Whymper, who took him as an apprentice for five years. After his apprenticeship he hired an attic as a studio and worked hard for the Illustrated London News. In December 1851 he made his first appearance in Punch.

Wolfgang Kilian belonged to the Kilian family of engravers in Augsburg and was the son of Bartholomaus Kilian the elder. His father died in 1583, after which his mother remarried and her new husband Dominicus Custos trained Wolfgang and his brother Lucas. From 1604 to 1608 he travelled in Italy and worked in Venice, Mantua and Milan. On his return he married and continued in the family workshop. His sons Bartholomaus the younger and Philipp also became engravers.

George Peter Alexander Healy grew up in Boston as the eldest of five children of an Irish merchant marine captain, and he helped support his mother after he lost his father. At sixteen he began drawing, and Jane Stuart lent him a painting by Guido that he copied and sold to a country priest. She introduced him to Thomas Sully, whose advice helped him. At eighteen he began painting portraits and was soon successful. In 1834 he went to Europe and stayed abroad for sixteen years, studying with Antoine-Jean Gros in Paris and coming under the influence of Thomas Couture.

Jacobus Buys, the son of an Amsterdam wig-maker, studied under Cornelis Pronk, then Jacob de Wit and Cornelis Troost. He ultimately became director of the Amsterdam Drawing Academy. He painted portraits, designed bas-reliefs and book illustrations, and made copies of works by the best masters of the seventeenth century, and in 1750 he joined Amsterdam's Guild of Saint Luke. Among his pupils was Cornelis Ploos van Amstel.

Carolus-Duran took his first drawing lessons from a sculptor at the Académie de Lille and then studied painting with François Souchon. He went to Paris in 1853, where he adopted the name Carolus-Duran, and had his first Salon exhibition in 1859. A scholarship from his hometown then took him to Rome and Spain, and he moved away from the Realism of Courbet toward Velázquez. On his return he won his first gold medal at the Salon. He became best known as a portrait painter of high society and as head of one of the principal ateliers in Paris.

Hablot Knight Browne, known by the pen name Phiz, illustrated books by Charles Dickens, Charles Lever, Augustus Septimus Mayhew and Harrison Ainsworth. He came from a family of French Huguenot ancestry whose surname was originally Bruneau, and he was born in Lambeth, near London, the fourteenth of fifteen children. When he was seven, his father abandoned the family. According to his biographer Valerie Browne Lester, Phiz was in fact the illegitimate son of his putative eldest sister Kate and a captain of Napoleon's Imperial Guard.

Ugo da Carpi worked as a printmaker between 1502 and 1532 in Venice, Rome and Bologna. He was the tenth of thirteen children of Count Astolfo da Panico, and he was known as Ugo Panico early in life before taking the name of his birthplace, Carpi. He claimed to be the first to use the chiaroscuro woodcut technique and sought copyright first from the Venetian senate and later from Pope Leo X. Although he did not invent it, he was one of its first Italian practitioners. He also produced a writing book and an altarpiece of Saint Veronica.

Nathaniel Currier founded the New York City printmaking business that became Currier and Ives. He was eight when his father died, and at fifteen he apprenticed in the Boston lithography shop of William and John Pendleton. The firm designed and sold inexpensive hand-painted lithographs based on news events, popular culture and Americana. It advertised itself as the Grand Central Depot for Cheap and Popular Prints, and in 1857 the name changed with the addition of James Merritt Ives. The Darktown Comics lithographs were among its best-selling works and depicted African Americans through racist caricatures.

Giambattista Pittoni studied under his uncle Francesco Pittoni, a well-known but undistinguished Venetian Baroque painter, and signed a Samson and Delilah together with him. He travelled little, and although he received many foreign commissions, records show him in Venice every year from 1720 onwards. His style changed from a heavy Baroque to a lighter and more delicate Rococo manner around that time. He was among the founders of the Academy of Fine Arts of Venice, and in 1758 he succeeded Tiepolo as its second president.

Piotr Michałowski grew up on an estate outside Kraków, the son of a landowner and senator of the Free City of Kraków. His talent developed at thirteen under several artists, including Michał Stachowicz and Franciszek Lampi. He studied classical philosophy, agriculture and mathematics at the Jagiellonian University. During the November Uprising he helped run a Polish munition factory, then escaped to Paris with his wife and her father. There he studied painting and anatomy with Nicolas Toussaint Charlet and was greatly influenced by Théodore Géricault. He is especially known for portraits and oil studies of horses.

William Beechey lost both parents in the early 1760s and grew up with his uncle, a solicitor in Chipping Norton, who wanted him to follow a career in law. He was entered as a clerk with a conveyancer but turned to painting instead. He entered the Royal Academy Schools, where he is thought to have studied under Johan Zoffany, and first exhibited at the Academy in 1776. His earliest surviving portraits are small-scale full-lengths and conversation pieces reminiscent of Zoffany. In 1782 he moved to Norwich, where he gained commissions including a series of civic portraits for the city's hall.

Isidore Pils, the son of a soldier, began studying with Guillaume Guillon-Lethière at twelve and in 1831 entered the École des Beaux-Arts under François-Édouard Picot. He won the Prix de Rome in 1838 for a history painting, then spent three years at the Villa Medici in Rome despite poor health. His earlier paintings have religious themes. After travelling with French troops through the Crimea, he turned to military and nationalistic subjects. His most famous work, Rouget de L'Isle Singing La Marseillaise, dates from 1849.

Thomas Stothard grew up in London as the son of an innkeeper in Long Acre. A delicate child, he was sent to Yorkshire at five, and later he was apprenticed to a draughtsman of patterns for brocaded silks in Spitalfields. In his spare time he attempted illustrations for his favourite poets, and James Harrison, editor of the Novelist's Magazine, praised some of them. After his master died he resolved to devote himself to art. He became a student of the Royal Academy in 1778 and a full academician in 1794.

Peter Michal Bohúň, the son of a Lutheran minister, attended the evangelical seminary in Levoča, where he embraced the idea of Slovak independence and earned the nickname Slavomil. After the seminary closed in 1841 he moved to Kežmarok, where he studied law. There he began to paint as a hobby. In 1843 he decided to become an artist and entered the Academy of Fine Arts in Prague, where Christian Ruben taught him. When his father died in 1844, he sought and obtained the patronage of a nobleman from Orava. He painted mainly portraits, along with landscapes and altarpieces.

Charles Balthazar Julien Févret de Saint-Mémin was educated at the École Militaire in Paris and served in the French Guards. During the Revolution his family travelled to Switzerland and then to New York City in 1793, intending to reach Saint-Domingue. News of that colony's fate made them stay, and after a failed attempt at raising vegetables he taught himself to make portraits. He lived in the United States until 1814 and often used the physiognotrace. His subjects included George Washington and Thomas Jefferson. He later served as museum director in Dijon.

John Frederick Kensett studied engraving with his English immigrant father, Thomas Kensett, and later with his uncle Alfred Daggett. He worked as an engraver in the New Haven area, then as a banknote engraver in New York City. His early work owed much to Thomas Cole but preferred cooler colors and less dramatic topography. His mature work shows tranquil scenery with a spare geometry, culminating in series where coastal promontories are balanced against glass-smooth water. He belonged to the second generation of the Hudson River School and was a founder of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Cornelis Saftleven came from a family of artists and probably learned to paint from his father Herman, alongside his brothers Abraham and Herman the Younger. After training in Rotterdam he likely travelled to Antwerp around 1632, and Rubens is known to have added figures to some of his paintings. When Rubens died in 1640, his collection held eight Saftlevens. Among his earliest works are portraits and peasant interiors influenced by Adriaen Brouwer. In Utrecht he and his brother began painting stable interiors, a new subject in peasant genre painting.

Adriaen van de Venne learned Latin in Leiden, according to Houbraken, then learned to paint from the goldsmith Simon de Valk and engraving from Jeronimus van Diest. In 1614 he moved to Middelburg, where he was influenced by Jan Brueghel the Elder and Pieter Brueghel the Elder. His painting Fishing for Souls comments ironically on the Catholic and Protestant troubles of the Eighty Years War. From 1620 until his death he made many grisailles and engravings of genre subjects, featuring peasants, beggars, thieves and fools as illustrations of current proverbs and sayings, mostly those of Jacob Cats.

Nils von Dardel came from the Swedish noble family von Dardel, and his grandfather Fritz von Dardel was a painter and adjutant to the later King Charles XV. He studied at the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts in Stockholm and became a member in 1934. Among his best-known paintings are The Dying Dandy, Crime Passionnel, Svarta Diana and John blund. In 1919 he proposed to Nita Wallenberg, but her father, a diplomat, disapproved of him. His work Exekution is said to be symbolic of that rejection.

Seneca Ray Stoddard was largely self-taught and left home at sixteen to paint ornamental freight cars and decorative scenes in passenger cars. He took up photography at twenty, first in Glens Falls and later throughout the Adirondacks. He was best known for his guidebook The Adirondacks: Illustrated, published in 1873 and reprinted through 1914, and for the first tourist map of the region. He also produced a topographical survey of the mountains. His writings and photographs helped popularize the Adirondacks.

Giuseppe Galli Bibiena, the second son of Ferdinando Galli Bibiena, accompanied his father to Barcelona for the wedding of Charles III of Habsburg. He later followed him to the court of Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, who hired Ferdinando as scenographer and painter. When his father left in 1717, Giuseppe became chief organizer of the court festivities and was named His Majesty's Second Theatrical Engineer. In 1723 he was promoted to First Theatrical Engineer, a position he kept until 1747. He also worked at Melk Abbey.

Olga Wisinger-Florian lived all her life in Vienna. She began private art lessons at nineteen but, frustrated with her progress, followed her parents' wishes and trained as a concert pianist with Julius Epstein. She had some success as a pianist from 1868 to 1873, until a hand injury forced her retirement. At thirty she returned to painting and studied first with August Schaeffer and then with Emil Jakob Schindler. She was one of only nine women asked to contribute to a 24-part encyclopedia of the Austro-Hungarian empire, and the only Austrian among them.

Pieter Coecke van Aelst came from Aalst, where his father was Deputy Mayor, and worked in Antwerp and Brussels. Karel van Mander wrote that he studied under Bernard van Orley, although no documents prove the apprenticeship. He became court painter to Charles V, and he also worked as an architect and designed woodcuts and tapestries. He was a polyglot. He published translations of Roman and Italian architectural treatises into Flemish, French and German, which spread Renaissance ideas in Northern Europe.

Hugo Darnaut was raised in Graz, the son of a court performer who used the stage name Darnaut. He began by studying decorative art in Vienna with a theater painter, then enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts. A scholarship took him to Düsseldorf, where he studied with the landscape painter Andreas Achenbach. He joined the Künstlerhaus in 1877. After Emil Jakob Schindler died, he took over the Schloss Plankenberg, where Schindler had run a school of landscape painting. In 1900 he helped create a monumental bird's-eye view of Vienna for the Exposition Universelle.

Kitao Shigemasa was the eldest son of the Edo bookseller Suharaya Mohei, and his family name was Kitabatake. He taught himself art before becoming a student of Nishimura Shigenaga. His early works are images of beautiful women in the style of Suzuki Harunobu. From 1765 he began illustrating books, which became his main focus, and over 250 are known. He has been called a chameleon who adapted to changing styles, and he was less active after the rise of Torii Kiyonaga. He was also noted for his haikai poetry and calligraphy.

Agnolo di Cosimo, known as Bronzino, lived all his life in Florence and from his late thirties was kept busy as court painter to Cosimo I de' Medici. He trained with Pontormo, whose style greatly influenced him, though his elegant, elongated figures stay calm and reserved, without the agitation of his teacher's. He was mainly a portraitist, but he also painted religious subjects and a few allegories, among them probably his best-known work, Venus, Cupid, Folly and Time. Many Medici portraits exist in several versions, because Cosimo sent copied portraits as diplomatic gifts.

Simon de Vlieger is mainly known for marine paintings, but he also painted beach scenes, landscapes and genre scenes. He was probably born in Rotterdam, and it is not known with whom he trained. His sister Neeltje also became a painter, specializing in still lifes. They both adopted De Vlieger, meaning the flyer, as an artist's surname, a common way to stand out. In 1627 he married Anna Gerrits van Willige, and in 1634 the family moved to Delft, where he joined the Guild of Saint Luke. In 1638 he moved to Amsterdam for a major project.

Pieter Claesz became a member of the Guild of Saint Luke in Berchem near Antwerp and moved to Haarlem, where his son, the landscape painter Nicolaes Berchem, was born. With Willem Claeszoon Heda he was a leading exponent of the ontbijt, or breakfast piece. They painted with subdued, almost monochromatic palettes, and the subtle handling of light and texture was their chief means of expression. Claesz generally chose more hospitable objects than Heda, though his later work became more colourful and decorative. His still lifes often suggest an allegorical purpose, with skulls as reminders of mortality.

Robert Bevan came from a Quaker family with long associations with Barclays Bank and was the fourth of six children. His first drawing teacher was Arthur Ernest Pearce, and in 1888 he studied under Fred Brown at the Westminster School of Art before moving to the Académie Julian in Paris, where Paul Sérusier and Pierre Bonnard were among his fellow students. He first visited Brittany with a fellow student, Eric Forbes-Robertson, in 1890. He married the Polish-born artist Stanisława de Karłowska. He was a founding member of the Camden Town Group, the London Group and the Cumberland Market Group.

Daniel Ridgway Knight studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris under Gleyre and later worked in Meissonier's private studio. After 1872 he lived in France, with a house and studio at Poissy on the Seine. He painted peasant women out of doors with great popular success, and he earned his first major distinction at the Salon of 1882 with his large oil Un Deuil. He later received the silver medal and the Cross of the Legion of Honor. He also competed as a sailor at the 1900 Summer Olympics. His son Louis Aston Knight became a landscape painter.

Albert Henry Payne was English by birth but lived and worked in Leipzig from 1839 onward. From the 1830s he made steel engravings of popular German destinations, which served a growing market for penny prints sold to tourists. Today he is best known for his 1840s engravings after paintings in the Dresden gallery, which Adolph Görling described in German essays. Payne published these essays in an illustrated bundle in 1848 and again in English as Royal Dresden Gallery. The book was quite popular, and a New York edition appeared in 1867.

Franz Hanfstaengl came from a commoner family and entered a drawing class in Munich on the recommendation of his town teachers. He learned lithography, met Alois Senefelder and studied at the Munich Academy of Fine Arts. In 1826 he went to Dresden and began copying the canvases of the Dresden Gallery in lithographs, a work completed in 1852. In 1833 he founded his own lithographic establishment in Munich, which later added a fine art printing shop and a photographic workshop. He won popularity as the portrait lithographer of Munich society.
